records.name: Monaco
records.summary:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. There is no functioning legal gender recognition process (ILGA-Europe lists Monaco among states without one), but that is a resident-facing gap: a visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever. Monaco is a tiny, heavily-policed, very low-crime tourist enclave embedded in France; street violence of any kind is rare.

No bathroom laws, no border friction (entry via France, Schengen rules), no documented anti-trans incidents. The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness (no LGR, limited explicit trans protections). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex intimacy legal but very few protections - cohabitation agreements only (no marriage or adoption); hate crimes/speech on sexual orientation penalised; no SOGISC discrimination ban; no legal procedure for name/gender change, though in 2022 a trans person changed markers via an affirmative court decision for the first time; no nonbinary recognition; IGM not banned; no official Pride; limited visibility.
GayVoyageur (in French): gay travel guide for Monaco - LGBT-friendly accommodation and destination information for the principality.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report for Monaco: no significant changes; significant issues limited to libel and lèse-majesté laws (not enforced); no torture, arbitrary detention or other abuses reported.

Nice-Matin via Monaco's Haut Commissariat (March 2025, in French): 'Transmission, filiation, congé parental, nationalité... les personnes LGBT face aux défis du quotidien à Monaco' - homosexuality decriminalised since the 18th century, yet Monaco ranks near the bottom of European LGBT-rights rankings; no equal succession, survivor pensions or parental leave; only ~10 people dare be out; Council of Europe rapporteur Béatrice Fresko-Rolfo: 'C'est le triste bilan de Monaco'.
Queer In The World: 'LGBT Rights In Monaco: Everything You Should Know Before You Visit' - country guide covering the legal situation and travel considerations.

records.name: Moldova
records.summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected of the former-Soviet states outside the Baltics. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity, and Chisinau Pride marches through the city centre under police protection. Moldova is on the EU accession path, driving continued legal alignment.

Counterweights: there is still no accessible legal gender recognition (a medicalised process exists on paper but Genderdoc-M reports it is not functional in practice), the Orthodox Church and major politicians (including Chisinau's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements, and the breakaway Russian-controlled region of Transnistria has its own anti-LGBT "propaganda" law — travelers should treat Transnistria as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Moldova: a trans woman was denied service at a bank due to document/appearance mismatch - the Equality Council confirmed discrimination; hate speech by politicians increased during election campaigns (Socialist Party newspaper: 'Ban on gay parades and LGBT propaganda in schools'); the location of GENDERDOC-M's Trans Camp was disclosed online, forcing relocation; hate crimes and domestic violence reported; civil society helped LGBT+ people fleeing Ukraine and Russia.

Amnesty International Moldova report 2025: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace; freedom of expression and assembly arbitrarily restricted; in Russian-occupied Transnistria new legislation prohibits 'promotion of non-traditional sexual relations'.

GENDERDOC-M report on the situation of LGBT+ rights in Moldova (2023): the Equality Council's 2022 study found extremely low acceptance - 79% of the population would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues; social distance score 5.7; marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022 amid pandemic, economic and security crises.
Attitude (Feb 2026): revisits Moldova Pride 2024 - a country slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity; participants of all ages and backgrounds join the festivities.

ECOM legislative analysis related to SOGI and HIV in Moldova (2024): identifies legal barriers affecting the quality of life of LGBT people and people living with HIV, based on a survey completed by local partners.

PinkNews (May 2018): police fired tear gas at anti-LGBT protesters to protect Moldova Pride in Chisinau; 20 embassies signed a statement of support for the march; President Dodon had publicly attacked the event the previous year.

PinkNews (March 2013): the Balti Court of Appeals struck down the city's 'homosexual propaganda' ban as unconstitutional and a human-rights violation, also criticising Balti's 'zone of enhanced support for the Orthodox Church' declaration - bans issued after church-led protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

records.name: Madagascar
records.summary: Madagascar demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal — unusual for the region — but France 24 documents that LGBT people must hide to keep jobs and live in peace; there is no LGR, no anti-discrimination law, and no visible community outside Antananarivo. No documented police targeting pattern.

sources.claim: France 24 'Focus' report (Aug 2024): 'LGBT people in Madagascar forced to hide their sexuality' — although homosexuality is not illegal, it is widely considered socially unacceptable; many hide to keep jobs and live in peace, developing their own networks and coded language.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Madagascar: documents the post-coup regime, unlawful killings, and 'societal discrimination and violence against women, persons with disabilities, and the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

BBC News Pidgin (July 2020): 'Homosexuality decriminalization and LGBT Rights in Africa' - overview of African nations that have decriminalised (Gabon joining ~22 of 53), with penalties of 10+ years elsewhere; regional context for Madagascar.
Queer In The World: 'LGBT Rights In Madagascar: Everything You Should Know Before You Visit' - country guide covering the legal situation (legal but unequal age of consent) and travel considerations.

Erasing 76 Crimes (July 2025): Madagascar rejected UN UPR recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech and to equalise the age of consent; six organisations (Queer Place, Mifoha Olo Mazoto, Divers' Unité, Justice Égalitaire, Men Engage, Madagascar LGBT+) protested: 'Refusing to act is to endorse impunity and condone violence.'

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Madagascar LGBTQI+ resources: legal framework - homosexual activity legal but Article 331 sets a different age of consent for same-sex acts; public attitudes, state protection capacity, case law, supporting organisations and country-of-origin experts.

records.name: Maldives
records.summary:
Maldives is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the Penal Code and sharia framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming Maldivians face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 HRC shadow report documents ICCPR violations). BUT: the tourist resort islands operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted on a resort; the risk concentrates in Malé and local islands.

A resort-only visit is lower-risk than the score suggests; any local-island contact raises it.

sources.claim: Human Rights Measurement Initiative Maldives 2024 summary: expert survey data - LGBTQIA+ people are among the groups most commonly identified as at risk of violations of empowerment rights; low scores on freedom of religion/belief (1.8/10), assembly (4.1) and expression (4.7).

Erasing 76 Crimes (Sept 2015): 'Maldives: Lenient no more, island nation arrests 2' - two men (56 and 27) arrested in their private home on Dhaandhoo for homosexual activity; the 2014 Penal Code extended criminalisation beyond Muslims to everyone, potentially punishable by death; Rainbow Warriors warned tourists could face similar threats.

UN OHCHR compilation (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/2, March 2015) for the Maldives' 2nd-cycle UPR: treaty-body and special-procedures information including reservations to ICCPR/CEDAW/CRC and human-rights concerns.

Maldives national UPR report (A/HRC/WG.6/22/MDV/1, April 2015): the government's own submission - development achievements, the 2014 Penal Code, and its handling of first-cycle recommendations (89 accepted, 20 rejected).

records.name: Mexico
records.summary:
Mexico pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Twenty-two of its 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Mexico City and Nayarit have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist.

Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the Americas after Brazil — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and central Mexico City, heavily policed and progressively governed, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is Mexico's general crime environment. Use the Admin Divisions view: state-level scores range from among Latin America's best (Mexico City) to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Mar 2025): 'Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges' — advances in legal gender recognition and hate-crime response alongside persistent violence and implementation gaps.

HRW report 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society' (March 2024) on the need for legal gender recognition in Tabasco, Mexico: murders and violence against trans people (e.g. Karina Gómez found in the Carrizal River with a concrete block tied to her feet, Aug 2023) rest on daily discrimination amplified by obstacles to legal name/gender recognition - the mismatch between lived and legal identities leaves trans people exposed.

The Guardian (July 2024): transfemicide becomes a crime in Mexico City - the 'Paola Buenrostro law' approved 18 July 2024, a 'watershed' moment named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

AP (Jan 2024): 'Wave of transgender killings in Mexico spurs protests' — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca shot in Mexico City, drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests.
IACHR press release (2024): the Inter-American Commission expressed concern over violence against trans and gender-diverse people in Mexico and urged protective measures.

Agencia Presentes (Jun 2024): 'Violence against trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders increased in the last year' in Mexico — data report on rising attacks against trans people and killings of defenders.

LSE USAPP commentary by Caroline Beer (Nov 2024): LGBTQ+ people in Mexico face significant threats of violence even as formal rights are extended - analysis of the gap between legal rights and lived safety.
Government of Canada travel advice for Mexico (updated Aug 2026): 'Exercise a high degree of caution' with regional advisories. General travel advice, not trans-specific.

Intrepid Travel country guide ('LGBTQIA+ travel in Mexico'): Mexico City has a large queer scene, annual Pride and LGBT-friendly hotels, bars and tours, plus Cancun as a hotspot; the guide also notes Mexico's indigenous 'third gender' muxes of Oaxaca and advises caution outside tourist hubs.

CNN en Español (July 2024): Mexico City's Congress approved the 'Paola Buenrostro' law criminalising transfemicide - the second federal entity to do so after Nayarit (March); named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

Mail & Guardian (Jan 2007): the northern Mexican state of Coahuila became the third Latin-American jurisdiction to approve gay civil unions (20-13 vote), following Mexico City and Buenos Aires - but the law bars same-sex couples from adopting or getting custody; PRI deputy Julieta Lopez called it 'a sensible response' to discrimination; PAN called it 'an attack against the family'.

records.name: Marshall Islands
records.summary: The Marshall Islands demands real caution. Same-sex conduct legal; US-associated; no LGR; no documented anti-trans pattern; very thin data. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust: 'A History of LGBT Criminalisation' - almost 500 years of outlawing LGBT people; overview of criminalising jurisdictions and strategic litigation (Marshall Islands context: no criminalisation).

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Marshall Islands: significant problems were prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence; no reports of torture, arbitrary killings or disappearances - no LGBT-specific abuses reported.

PSGDN Pacific LGBTQI Network, Marshall Islands page: profile of Anfernee Nenol Kaminaga, a 25-year-old pansexual genderqueer Marshall Islander who co-created and led 'Brighten the Rainbow' - known as the first openly LGBTIQ initiative in the Marshall Islands; also a UNESCO Youth Ambassador and UN Youth Climate Action Summit representative.

records.name: North Macedonia
records.summary:
North Macedonia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised, and Skopje hosts both Pride and an organised Trans March for Visibility (TransFormA, March 2024) — public trans organising that proceeds without serious incident. Anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity (2019 amendments). Counterweights: hate speech and hate crimes remain common with no effective justice-system response (European Commission), social-media death threats are routine, and there is no legal gender recognition.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; small but functioning community; standard Balkan street-hostility caution.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on North Macedonia: hate speech remained serious with no meaningful state response despite countless reports (echoed by the European Commission's country report); in September the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist, applying SOGI aggravating grounds; ECRI called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries; anti-gender movement gained ground, including campaigns against a school handout showing a gay couple.

Global Voices (March 2024): 'We march bravely' - Transgender Day of Visibility marked in North Macedonia with a March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje organised by TransFormA; notes a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

ILGA-Europe/ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024: country submissions from Western Balkans and Eastern Partnership countries (including North Macedonia) with top priorities, feedback on the European Commission's 2023 Enlargement Report, and recommendations to the EU.
US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for North Macedonia: official assessment including the SOGI section - anti-discrimination law, societal violence and discrimination against LGBT persons.
Washington Blade (Oct 2023): 'Anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms economies of Serbia, North Macedonia' - economic analysis of the cost of discrimination in the Balkans.

Balkan Insight (Feb 2012): ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Europe Index put Macedonia at the bottom of the Balkans with a score of -2 (scale 17 to -7) - the only Balkan country in the 'red zone' of worst offenders, characterised by 'gross violations of human rights and discrimination'.

Balkan Insight (July 2014): Macedonia's government submitted a constitutional motion to define marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman, ruling out same-sex marriage and gay adoption - needing two-thirds of MPs, with the conservative DPA expected to provide the extra votes.

records.name: Mali
records.summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Nov 2024): 'New Mali Law Disastrous for LGBT People' — the 2024 penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with harsh penalties.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Mali's new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Conversation (Jan 2025), interview with anthropologist Christophe Broqua: Mali's new penal code (announced October 2024, in effect 13 December 2024) criminalises homosexuality and any citizen seen to encourage it - a sharp escalation under the military junta, alongside clampdowns on opposition and media.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Mali: official assessment - same-sex conduct not criminalised but significant societal stigma; violence and instability from armed groups.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Mali: documents gender inequality, FGM, corruption, and 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' among other human-rights problems.
